ch26.title: The Eleven Scattered
ch26.src: Paper 139 (the later lives of the apostles); parts of Papers 194–196
ch26.b002: Andrew began to write very soon after the Master vanished on Olivet. At night he would drag a lamp into a corner of the upper chamber in the Marks’ house, set a board across his knees, and spread a scrap of parchment on it. The reed pen did not sit well in his thick fingers. They were hands that had mended nets. More than once he spilled the ink, and more than once he began again from the beginning.
ch26.b003: He wrote down what the Master had said and what he had done. The first day they walked together by the Jordan, the wedding feast at Cana, the winter grass on the highland, the mornings by the lake, the bread for five thousand, the night in Gethsemane. He wrote as he remembered, and only as much as he remembered. He did not embellish. That was his way. Just as he had never spoken aloud of a thing he was not sure of, he did not write down a thing he was not sure of.
ch26.b004: Once his pen stopped for a long time before the name of Judas Iscariot. He did not know what to write about that man. Everyone knew what he had done. But why he had come to it, when something inside him had first begun to bend away, no one knew. Andrew had been the first to see that bending, and he had told no one. In the end he wrote down only the Master’s words to Judas: the warnings, and the kind words the Master never once withdrew. To the very end the Master had treated Judas exactly as he treated the rest of them. That much Andrew knew for certain, and so that much he could write.
ch26.b005: Now and then he set down his pen and looked round the room. The breathing of his sleeping brethren lay evenly over the dark. He went from face to face. It was an old habit. He wanted to write about them as well: how Peter had stood in the temple court, how Thomas had knelt in the shut room, how the twins had fallen asleep beside the fire on the night of the ordination. But he did not write it. That was not the Master’s story. And he was still a man who could not easily bring out a word of praise for his brethren, whether with a pen or with his tongue. Once, by the pool of Siloam on the night of Pentecost, he had got past that hardness in himself. It felt as though he had spent a lifetime’s share of it in one evening.
ch26.b006: So his record holds no story of the eleven. After his death it was copied again and again and passed among the early teachers of the church; it was edited and changed and added to until it had become a fairly connected account of the Master’s life. And about a hundred years after the first pages were written, the last of those copies perished in a fire at Alexandria. No one can read that parchment now. So here, then, is the story his record left out, the story he never wrote: the story of his brethren.
ch26.b008: After Pentecost the eleven quietly began to scatter. No one quarreled. It was only that each man began to see his own road.
ch26.b009: The Alpheus twins went home to Galilee. Their work was done. They were not made for the tangled struggles of building the kingdom, and they knew it. On the shore the Master had told them that even if they went back to their old work, they must never let a change in what their hands did shake their loyalty. They lived by that. They cast their nets again, raised their children, sat by the lake in the evenings. Not for a moment did they forget that for four years they had lived close beside the one who had made a universe. To the end they wore cheerfully the nickname they had been given: the least of all the apostles.
ch26.b010: Simon Zelotes went nowhere for a time. He kept to himself. Thomas too was troubled for a while, but his time of trouble was shorter than Simon’s. He soon took up teaching again, and he gave the apostles wise counsel. He was always the one who saw the danger first. But once a decision was made, he was still the first man on his feet.
ch26.b011: Nathaniel clashed more and more with Peter. The Master had told them to preach the Father’s kingdom; why, then, were they preaching only the Master himself? He could not let the question go. By the middle of the following month the rift between them had grown so wide that Nathaniel quietly withdrew and went to Philadelphia, to Abner and Lazarus. About that time his aged father died. He stayed in Philadelphia more than a year and then went on into the lands beyond Mesopotamia, carrying the gospel as he understood it.
ch26.b012: Matthias, the new apostle, took little part in what came after. He held the purse; that was his share.
ch26.b013: And so of the original twelve, only six were left to play their part when the gospel was first proclaimed in Jerusalem: Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, and Matthew. Soon after Pentecost the Master’s mother went back to Salome’s home at Bethsaida. John saw her off and stood waving a long time.
ch26.b014: Day after day the believers met with one heart in the temple and broke bread in their homes. They called each other brother and sister and looked after the poor. Many sold what they owned and shared it in common, because they were firmly convinced the Master would return within their own generation. As the years went by, the shared goods ran out, but the world did not end. Before long the believers at Antioch would be taking up a collection to keep their brethren in Jerusalem from starving. Through it all Peter stood at the front. People looked to him as their head, and no one contested the place. Andrew organized the work at his side. The man who had once been chief of the twelve now helped with his brother’s work, and he did not find that strange in the least.
ch26.b015: For a while Jerusalem was quiet. The Sadducees threw some of the leaders into prison, but the rabbi Gamaliel restrained them: if this work came from men it would fall of itself, he said, and if it came from God no one could stop it. Because of his counsel, peaceful days followed. Then many Greeks came in from Alexandria, and among their converts were men like Stephen. Stephen preached more nearly as the Master had taught, and one day, in the middle of a sermon, men stoned him to death without even the form of a trial. Within a month of Stephen’s death the church at Jerusalem was organized under Peter’s leadership, and James, the Master’s brother, was made its titular head. Andrew did not forget what the Master had asked of him on the shore: when the brethren scattered, he was to be a wise counselor to the Master’s brother, who would be loaded with burdens he had no experience to bear.
ch26.b017: Of the eleven, the first to go was James Zebedee.
ch26.b018: On that morning by the sea, the Master had told James to be less impatient with his brethren. He had told him to pray for a quiet spirit and to cultivate patience, for these would hold him up when the time came to drink the cup of sacrifice. And he had told him never to be dismayed. James did not forget.
ch26.b019: Years before, when his mother had asked the Master to seat her two sons at his right hand and his left, the Master had asked them whether they could drink the cup he would drink. They said they could. For James that answer came true to the letter. Herod Agrippa feared him more than any other apostle. James was usually quiet, but when his convictions were challenged he would not give an inch. He was put to death with the sword.
ch26.b020: He bore his last day with grace. One man who had attended his trial and execution, his own accuser and informer, was so shaken by the sight that he ran from the place where James died and joined the disciples of Jesus. The son of thunder who had once wanted to call fire down from heaven lit a fire, at the last, in the heart of the man who had accused him.
ch26.b021: When the news of James reached Andrew, he was silent a long time. They had been partners, hauling nets together at the Bethsaida landing. On the day of the ordination, when the hand rested on his head, James had been wrapped in a silence that seemed full to the brim. Andrew thought that silence must have kept him to the very end. He did not open his record that night. He only corrected, in his heart, the count he had kept of their names, from eleven to ten.
ch26.b022: James’s early death did much to soften the fierce temper of his younger brother, and as the years went on John’s temper grew quieter and more controlled still. Several years after James’s death, John married his brother’s widow and took on the care of his brother’s household.
ch26.b024: When persecution broke out, the believers abandoned Jerusalem and the apostles scattered in every direction. In choosing the first missionaries to be sent out in those days, Peter, James and John relied on no one’s counsel more than Andrew’s. He had an eye for the gifts hidden in young people. The eye for men remained his to the end.
ch26.b025: Philip was the first apostle to go beyond the bounds of the Jews.
ch26.b026: On the shore the Master had told him to go into the lands of the gentiles. He would no longer be tied down with money and supplies, the Master had said, and he must stop being afraid of men. The steward who had spent years reckoning the meals of thirteen men did as he was told. He went down into Samaria and preached and baptized those who believed. Only, he held back from laying his hands on them as a sign that they had received the Spirit of Truth. It was the same caution that had always sent him to Andrew whenever he could not recall his instructions. That was done by Peter and John, who came down from Jerusalem. After the resurrection Philip baptized his whole family of seven. His wife, who had served in the women’s corps, was a fearless woman. On the last day she stood at the foot of her husband’s cross and urged him to proclaim the good news even to the men who were killing him. When his strength gave out, she took up the story of salvation herself, and she stopped only when the furious crowd fell on her and stoned her. Philip was buried at Hierapolis. Their eldest daughter, Leah, carried on their work. She was the daughter of the man whose rare gift was simply to say, Come.
ch26.b027: Matthew went north: Syria, Cappadocia, Galatia, Bithynia, Thrace.
ch26.b028: On the shore the Master had told him that he would no longer supply his brethren with the things of daily life but would himself proclaim the good news. He had told him to remember that Jew and gentile alike were his brothers. There had been days when Matthew stayed to listen to the teaching instead of going out to raise the week’s money, and then quietly made up the shortfall out of his own purse. Now he took that teaching and went out on the road with it. He left with his hands nearly empty. His small fortune had long since run out. For four years, whenever the apostolic purse ran low, he had secretly filled it with his own money, given in the names of other believers, because he feared his brethren would shrink from a publican’s money. Whenever he was looked down upon, he burned to tell them, but he never did. He only wished the Master might know. He little realized that the Master had known everything from the beginning. And the other apostles never knew. Not one of the eleven ever learned whose purse had paid for so much of the bread they had eaten; each died in his own land without knowing. Not even Andrew knew. The best judge of men among them never saw through this one thing. Matthew died at Lysimachia in Thrace, through a plot that certain unbelieving Jews made with Roman soldiers. His brethren never heard of it. The notes he had kept of the Master’s sayings became the basis of the gospel that Isador later put together. Somewhere among them, surely, was the saying about not letting the left hand know what the right hand does.
ch26.b029: Thomas crossed the islands: Cyprus, Crete, the coast of North Africa, Sicily. Everywhere he went he preached and baptized. To a doubter, the words of one who had doubted carried best.
ch26.b030: On the shore the Master had told him to stop doubting, to believe like a child but stop acting like one. Doubt was the guest of his whole life. But he no longer handed that guest the keys to his house. He was arrested by agents of the Roman government in Malta and put to death. Only a few weeks before he died, he had begun to write down the life and teachings of the Master. The man who had measured and recorded everything set out, at the very end, to record the one man he had never been able to measure.
ch26.b031: After the persecution scattered them, Simon Zelotes broke down once more. He was a nationalist who had laid his dream down before the Master’s teaching, and now it seemed that everything was lost. For some years he hid himself away in despair. But he rose again. He went to Alexandria, worked his way up the Nile, and pressed on into the heart of Africa, preaching and baptizing until he was old and feeble. Peace on earth, good will among men: when he first heard such words he had thought they could come only after victory. Instead of a sword, he carried them into the very heart of Africa. There he died, and there he was buried.
ch26.b032: Nathaniel went through Mesopotamia and on as far as India. He preached and baptized there, and in India he died. The man who could move from philosophy to poetry and then, without warning, to a joke: where and how his life ended, his brother apostles never learned. The one among the eleven who had made them laugh most vanished most quietly of all.
ch26.b033: On the shore the Master had told Nathaniel to mix friendship into his counsel and add love to his philosophy, and to expect less of some men so as to be less disappointed. Perhaps he remembered those words when he and Peter parted. He did not leave in a quarrel. He withdrew quietly and went his own way.
ch26.b035: After Peter left Jerusalem, he traveled among the churches from Babylon to Corinth. His wife went with him on every road. He was the first apostle to stand up for Philip among the Samaritans and for Paul among the gentiles. Yet at Antioch, before Judaizers who mocked him, he drew back for a time from the gentile believers. The man who would face a sword head-on was still weak before ridicule at his back. Paul rebuked him without fear. Even so, in their later years the two of them worked together in building up the churches.
ch26.b036: He was the outstanding preacher of the twelve. Aside from Paul, no one did more to build up the kingdom and send its messengers out to every corner of the earth within a single generation. Luke wrote down parts of some of his sermons, and his teaching runs through the Gospel of Mark. His vigorous voice lived on in his letter, at least until a disciple of Paul altered it. The hoarse voice that first broke out in the temple court on the day of Pentecost traveled across many lands in this way.
ch26.b037: To the day of his death Peter carried a confusion in one corner of his mind. Jesus as the Messiah of the Jews, Christ as the redeemer of the world, the Son of Man who showed men the Father of all: the three never quite settled into one inside him. But he kept the words he had been given on the shore. Feed my sheep. Follow me to the end.
ch26.b038: In Rome his captors told him that he must die as his Master had died, on a cross. Peter took it as a high honor. The man who in the courtyard of Annas had denied that name at a serving girl’s word was glad, at the last, to hang on the same kind of tree for that name. On the day he died, his wife was thrown to the wild beasts in the arena at Rome.
ch26.b040: Andrew traveled through Armenia, Asia Minor and Macedonia. He was no famous preacher. Standing before great crowds was never his part. He was a man who sat down across from one person and talked. Just as, by the Jordan, he had first gone to find one person, his brother. One by one in that way he brought many thousands into the kingdom. Everywhere he went, people called him Simon Peter’s brother. All his life he never minded.
ch26.b041: He was seized at Patrae in Achaia and crucified. He was a robust man. It took two full days for him to die. Through those two days he went on proclaiming from the cross the good news of the kingdom of heaven. The man who had been sparing with words, who all his life had swallowed every word of praise before it left his throat, spoke without ceasing for two days at the end.
ch26.b042: On the shore the Master had told him to go on trusting; the Master would not fail him, and when Andrew’s work on earth was done he would come to him. Andrew never asked for that promise to be proved. Proof was Thomas’s affair. He simply trusted it and worked to the end. That was his way.
ch26.b043: What he thought about in those two days, no one knows. But he was surely still a man who counted heads. How many stood beneath the cross, who wept and who mocked, who would go home that night and tell the story to someone else. And perhaps he counted other faces as well: his brother, who would be in Rome; John in Ephesus; Simon somewhere beyond the desert; Nathaniel and Matthew, of whom there was no word. He did not know where all of them were. Still, he would have gone through them one by one, to make sure no one was missing. That was the chief’s work. The chief was always the one who checked last.
ch26.b045: Of the eleven, the one who lived longest was John, the youngest.
ch26.b046: He was the one apostle who went right along with the Master on the night of the arrest. He stayed near the cross to the end, took the Master’s mother into his care, and of all the twelve was the first truly and fully to believe in the resurrection. On the shore the Master had told him to give up his intolerance, to learn to love men, to devote his life to showing that love is greatest. He gave that work more than seventy years.
ch26.b047: He was imprisoned several times, and he was banished to the isle of Patmos for four years, until another emperor came to power in Rome. On that island he wrote the Book of Revelation. He did not collide head-on with the authorities as his brother James had. Together with James the Lord’s brother, he learned before magistrates that a soft answer turns away wrath. They described the church less as the kingdom of heaven than as a spiritual brotherhood devoted to serving mankind. They taught loving service rather than ruling power.
ch26.b048: He became bishop of the churches of Asia and settled at Ephesus. For the last twenty years of his life a loving granddaughter cared for him. At ninety-nine he directed his associate Nathan in writing the gospel that bears his name. In it he called himself, more than once, the disciple whom Jesus loved. It was the hidden conceit of his youth, come back a little in old age, but no one need blame him for it. He truly was the one the Master had so often trusted.
ch26.b049: At the last, when he could no longer stand in the pulpit, he was carried to church in a chair. When the service was ending and the people asked him to say a few words, for years he said only one thing: My little children, love one another. That was what the young man who had wanted to call down fire from heaven left behind at the end. John died quietly at Ephesus in A.D. 103, at the age of one hundred and one.
ch26.b051: Andrew’s parchment was burned. Thomas died just after he began to write. Matthew’s notes were put together by another man’s hand into a book that bears another name. In John’s gospel the memories of the old apostle are mingled with the hand of the one who wrote them down. What the eleven wrote was scattered and changed and lost.
ch26.b052: But what they left behind was not writing. On the winter grass of the highland the Master had told them that men would know they had been with him not so much by their words as by their lives. And so it was. In a village in Armenia, on a hillside at Hierapolis, in some nameless settlement far up the Nile, on a riverbank in India, people remembered not so much the words of the eleven as their faces. A fisherman’s cracked hands, an unhurried step, a gaze that did not turn away even from an enemy.
ch26.b053: Twelve commonplace men. When the Master called them that on the highland, Nathaniel had nearly laughed out loud. Fishermen with cracked hands, a steward who knew only how to keep accounts, a publican, a Zealot, a gloomy stonemason, and those twins. One of them lost his way. The other eleven walked to the end. They were scattered, and they died each in his own land, not knowing how the others had ended.
ch26.b054: Did the twins in Galilee hear the news, one report after another? If they did, they likely sat side by side by the lake and wept with the same face at the same moment. And the next morning they would have taken up their nets and gone out on the water again. On the shore the Master had told them to keep believing, even if they went back to their old work, and to remember the days they had spent together. They did. On the night of the ordination, when they had fallen asleep beside the fire, he had said they were doing well and should not be woken. And they were never alone. The one who came into the upper chamber on the day of Pentecost had not left their side from that day on.
ch26.b056: The later lives of the apostles follow the closing paragraphs of each section of Paper 139: Andrew’s private record and the fate of its copies, his counsel in choosing the first missionaries, “Simon Peter’s brother,” his travels in Armenia, Asia Minor and Macedonia, and his two days on the cross at Patrae (139:1.7–9, 1.12); Peter’s preaching and writings, his journeys and the Antioch episode, his confusion of mind, his wife, and his crucifixion in Rome (139:2.7, 2.9, 2.11–15); James’s martyrdom and the conversion of his accuser (139:3.5, 3.8–9); John’s faithfulness at the cross, his marriage and granddaughter, his exile on Patmos, Ephesus and Nathan’s gospel, “love one another,” and his natural death in A.D. 103 at one hundred and one, with his temper subdued in later years (139:4.4, 4.6–7, 4.10, 4.12–15); Philip in Samaria, his family, his wife’s death, his daughter Leah, and Hierapolis (139:5.4, 5.9–12); the death of Nathaniel’s father and Nathaniel’s death in India (139:6.9); Matthew’s hidden generosity and penniless departure, his northern mission and death at Lysimachia, and his notes (139:7.5, 7.8–10); Thomas’s island mission, his execution in Malta, and the writing begun weeks before his death (139:8.13); the twins’ return home and lifelong honor (139:9.5, 9.11); Simon Zelotes’s collapse and his mission in Africa (139:11.6, 11.10–11).
ch26.b057: The scattering after Pentecost, the six who remained, the rift between Nathaniel and Peter, Matthias, and Mary’s return home are from 193:6.1, 6.3–5; the common life of the first believers and the end of their shared goods from 194:4.3, 4.7; Gamaliel, Stephen, and the Jerusalem church under Peter with James the Lord’s brother from 194:4.10–12; the Master’s words on the shore to John, James, Andrew, Thomas, Nathaniel, Philip, Matthew and the twins from 192:2.1, 2.7–13; the question of the cup from 139:3.8; the twins asleep by the fire from 140:6.14. The closing thought of “lives, not words” follows the ordination address (140:1.7).
ch26.b058: Added as fiction: Andrew writing in a corner of the upper chamber and his choice not to write about his brethren; his hesitation over the name of Judas; Andrew hearing of James’s death; the imagined reckoning of faces on the cross at Patrae; the twins’ daily life after their return and how they might have taken the news; John waving Mary off; and the narrator’s reflections linking each man’s end. The text names only James as the first of the apostles to die, so no other order of deaths is set.
ch26.b059: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
